newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - U.S. bull market celebrates a birthday.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - U.S. bull market celebrates a birthday.

text.p: Wall Street's raging bull celebrated a birthday on Tuesday, but not all investors agreed on how many candles to put on the cake.
Some on Wall Street date the birth of the current bull run to August 12, 1982, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average touched down at 777.
But others see a much younger rally, dating from late 1994, with legs to carry it into the next century.
Still others date the current trend from late 1990 after the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait sent stocks in a tailspin, arguing that the bull is living on borrowed time.
Investors on Tuesday did not exactly pop champagne for the bull's birthday. The Dow industrials, tumbled 101 points to close at 7961.

Those in the 15-year birthday camp see a long-term trend line rising from August 12, 1982, puctuated but not broken by notable corrections in 1984, 1987, 1990 and 1994. In the 15-year run the Dow has climbed about 930 percent.

However, Prudential Securities technical analyst Ralph Acampora bases his bull market thesis, which anticipated the Dow breaking 7,000 and sees 10,000 possible by June 1998, on the view that the bull market was born in November 1994.

"A typical secular bull market lasts several years (perhaps three to four years, but certanly more than two-and-a-half years)," he wrote in a recent research note. "Therefore, I believe 12-18 months remain in this bull's run."
Gregory Nie, technical analyst at EVEREN Securities, said he viewed the move begun in late 1994 as the "primary trend."
Because of the advances in communications and the global nature of the stock market, timeframes for market trends have been compressed, he said.
"The reaction time to catalysts has shrunk dramatically," Nie said.

Some analysts argue there may actually be two bull market trends running concurrently. They cite a short-term "cyclic" move based on factors such as interest rates, price/earnings ratios and currency fluctuations, and a longer-term "secular" trend, based on broader macro-economic issues such as the effort to balance the U.S. budget.

The average cyclic bull market from the 1950s has lasted about 35-1/2 months, which would leave a bull run started in late 1994 little time left, said John Brooks, director of marketing at Notley Information Service, which provides technical analysis on global markets.
"This particular cyclic bull market is probably long in the tooth and is about to give up the ghost," Brooks said, adding that 1998 could be a bear-market year.
But the longer-term trend may still remain intact.
"The longer-term secular move probably has another wave in it to the year 2001 or so," he said.

Then there are those who argue that the question of the bull market's age is academic and does not address traditional signals of a potential market top such as current elevated price earnings ratios and low dividend yields.
"Whether this thing is three-and-a-half years old, 10 years old or 15 years old really doesn't matter," said Ralph Bloch, chief technical analyst at Raymond James & Associates.
Whatever its age, the bull market has defied many on Wall Street who have tried to chart its demise and it may continue to do so.
"Once you run off the historical charts anything can happen," said Bob Dickey, technical analyst at Dain Bosworth.
